extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators, and jurors (users of jury instructions in U.S. patent trials)
extracted.subtask_description: Model post-trial/jury instructions for evaluating patent infringement and invalidity issues in U.S. federal court, describing legal standards, elements, burdens, and illustrative factors for jury findings. Intended to be used when instructing juries or drafting jury instruction language for patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents — equivalency test
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim requirement is satisfied under the doctrine of equivalents if the accused [part/step of the product/method] performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result as the claim requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may consider whether, at the time of the alleged infringement, persons of ordinary skill in the field would have known of the interchangeability of the [part/step] with the claimed requirement. Interchangeability at the present time is not sufficient. Known interchangeability is not necessary to find infringement under the doctrine of equivalents but may support a conclusion that the difference is not substantial. The patent holder must prove equivalency by a preponderance of the evidence. You may not apply the doctrine of equivalents to claim elements that were in the prior art or would have been obvious, or to subject matter that was described in the patent specification but not claimed if it was specific enough that one of ordinary skill would understand it was present in the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims — literal infringement (35 U.S.C. §112(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A means-plus-function requirement covers only the specific structure disclosed in the patent specification for performing the claimed function and the equivalents of those specific structures; it does not cover all possible structures that could perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge will identify the structure in the specification that corresponds to the means-plus-function requirement. Jurors must first decide whether the accused product has any structure that performs the specific function; if not, the claim is not infringed. If it does, determine whether that structure is the same as or equivalent to the structure identified in the specification. To prove equivalence, the patent holder must show that a person of ordinary skill would have considered the differences insubstantial at the time the patent issued or that the structures/actions performed the function in substantially the same way to accomplish substantially the same result. In assessing interchangeability, the interchangeability must have been known at the time the patent issued and the structure must have been available then. If a method claim uses step-plus-function, substitute 'acts' for 'structure' accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on the doctrine of equivalents due to prosecution disclaimer/amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent holder made certain claim changes or statements during prosecution, the doctrine of equivalents analysis cannot be applied to those claim requirements that were disclaimed or limited during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a list of the specific requirements (on a claim-by-claim basis) that the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to. Unless each of these requirements is literally present in the accused product/method, there can be no infringement of the claim as to those requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement — elements (35 U.S.C. §271(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement can arise when someone supplies something that is used to infringe one or more patent claims. Someone other than the supplier must directly infringe a claim; if there is no direct infringement by anyone, there can be no contributory infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holder must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) the alleged infringer sells, offers to sell, or imports within the U.S. a component of a product or apparatus for use in a process during the patent term; (2) the component or apparatus has no substantial, noninfringing use; (3) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the invention; (4) at the time of supplying the component, the alleged infringer is aware of the patent or believed there was a high probability a patent existed and deliberately avoided learning of it; (5) at the time of supplying, the alleged infringer knows the component was especially made or adapted for use in infringing the patent or believed there was a high probability and deliberately avoided learning the infringing nature; and (6) the component has been used to directly infringe the claim. Define “non-infringing use” as a use other than as a component of the patented product or in the patented method that is not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducing infringement — elements (35 U.S.C. §271(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Inducement requires that someone else actually directly infringe a claim; there can be no inducement without direct infringement. The alleged inducer is liable only if the patent holder proves specific elements by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holder must prove: (1) the allegedly infringing acts are actually carried out by the alleged direct infringer and directly infringe the claim; (2) the alleged infringer took action during the patent term intending to cause the infringing acts by the direct infringer; and (3) the alleged infringer was aware of the patent and knew that the acts, if taken, would constitute infringement. For willful blindness issues, alternatives permit findings where the alleged infringer believed there was a high probability of infringement and deliberately avoided learning of it. In deciding inducement, you may consider whether the accused infringer actually believed the acts did not infringe and whether it relied on advice of counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — subjective prong (standard and factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Willfulness requires that the patent holder show it is highly probable that, prior to the filing date of the complaint, the alleged infringer acted with reckless disregard of the patent claims. Willfulness is judged by clear and convincing evidence. The jury is limited to the subjective prong; the objective prong (whether a reasonable person would have considered there to be a high likelihood of infringement) is a matter of law for the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To demonstrate ‘reckless disregard,’ the patent holder must persuade the jury that the alleged infringer actually knew, or it was so obvious that it should have known, that its actions constituted infringement. Consider all facts including: factors that suggest non-willfulness (acting consistent with industry standards, making a good-faith effort to avoid infringing such as designing around the patent; reliance on a well-supported opinion of counsel if invoked) and factors suggesting willfulness (intentional copying of a patented product; attempts to cover up infringement). The Committee does not recommend seeking an advisory opinion on the objective prong from the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove invalidity of any patent claim, the alleged infringer must persuade the jury that it is highly probable that the claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the heightened standard associated with challenges to validity (clear and convincing/highly probable). Follow case authorities cited (e.g., Microsoft v. i4i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the specification does not contain an adequate written description demonstrating that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention at the time the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to meet the written description requirement. The requirement is satisfied if a person of ordinary skill reading the original application would have recognized that the application described the invention as claimed; exact wording is unnecessary and missing claim limitations can be valid if necessarily implied to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. §112(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a sufficiently full and clear description to allow a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention at the time of the original filing without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the patent is not enabling. In assessing undue experimentation, consider: (1) scope of the claimed invention; (2) amount of guidance in the patent; (3) amount of experimentation necessary; (4) time and cost of necessary experimentation; (5) how routine the experimentation is in the field; (6) whether the patent discloses specific working examples; (7) nature and predictability of the field; and (8) level of ordinary skill in the art. No single factor is dispositive — weigh them in context of the invention and state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art — definitions and effect of examiner consideration (pre- and post-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art may include publicly known or available knowledge, uses, offers for sale, publications, or patents that disclose the claimed invention or elements thereof. Definitions differ depending on priority date relative to March 16, 2013 (AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims with priority before March 16, 2013: prior art must have been made/known/used/published/patented before the invention or more than one year before filing; inventor's own publication less than one year before invention is not prior art. For claims with priority on/after March 16, 2013: prior art is material made/known/used/published/patented before the effective filing date or described in an earlier-filed published patent/application naming another inventor. Exceptions include disclosures by the inventor (within one year) or subject matter obtained from the inventor, and certain common-ownership exceptions. When a challenger relies on prior art considered by the Examiner during prosecution, the challenger bears a greater burden to overcome deference to the agency; prior art not considered by the Examiner may be given more weight. If invention date or date of prior art is disputed, jury must determine conception vs reduction to practice and diligence; definitions of conception and reduction to practice are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — not new / single-reference requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid as anticipated if all of its requirements existed in a single device, method, publication, or patent that predates the claimed invention (or the effective filing date post-AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged infringer must prove anticipation by clear and convincing evidence. The single reference need not use the same words as the claim, but all claim requirements must be present, stated or necessarily implied, so that a person of ordinary skill could make and use the claimed invention from that one reference. Illustrative ways to show lack of novelty include prior public knowledge/use in the U.S., prior patents or printed publications anywhere in the world, prior making by another in the U.S. (if not abandoned/secret), certain prior U.S. patents or published applications, or evidence that the named inventor learned the invention from another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bars — timeliness of filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the patent application was not filed within the time required by law (a statutory bar): all claim requirements must have been present in one prior art reference dated more than one year before the application filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claim is invalid due to a statutory bar. Prior art for this purpose can include the inventor’s own work, use, or commercialization efforts. The instruction provides a list of ways to show the application was not timely filed (select applicable items for the case).
